summary:
This evaluation covered 5 chat-based tasks related to AWS Bedrock/SageMaker evaluation monitoring and triage, with 10 total iterations (1 per variant per eval) and no failed runs. Quality-comparison pairs were skipped in every eval (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped each), so no head-to-head output-quality judgments or run-to-run consistency data are available for either variant — that dimension is simply absent evidence, not a result in favor of either side.

On expected-output match, with_skill met the expected output in 3 of 5 evals (evaluation-coverage-assessment, finish-reason-truncation-drift, quality-regression-triage) while without_skill met it in 0 of 5. In the remaining two evals (sagemaker-eval-routing-and-failure, bedrock-native-eval-job-failed) neither variant met the expected output, though confidence on those two was medium/high, suggesting the task or expectation itself may be difficult to satisfy rather than indicating a close call. Where with_skill did meet expectations, confidence was high to medium; where without_skill failed to meet them, confidence was medium, so these are moderate- rather than low-confidence findings.

Per-assertion pass rates follow a similar pattern: with_skill outscored without_skill in three evals (6/6 vs 2/6 in evaluation-coverage-assessment; 3/5 vs 1/5 in finish-reason-truncation-drift; 5/6 vs 1/6 in sagemaker-eval-routing-and-failure), the two tied at 3/3 in quality-regression-triage, and with_skill still led in bedrock-native-eval-job-failed (4/6 vs 3/6). Some individual assertions passed for both variants (e.g., citing a concrete cause, addressing A/B comparison, recommending a specific gate) — these are not differentiating. Others failed for both variants across evals (e.g., stating whether invocation logging is enabled, giving both current and baseline figures, citing an evaluation check-id in bedrock-native-eval-job-failed, and avoiding exposure of a raw 12-digit account ID in that same eval) — these point to shared gaps in behavior or possibly assertions that are hard to satisfy regardless of variant. One assertion ("No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed" in sagemaker-eval-routing-and-failure) passed for without_skill but failed for with_skill, the only case where without_skill outperformed with_skill on an individual assertion.

On runtime and cost, without_skill was consistently faster and cheaper than with_skill across all five evals — for example 24s/$0.20 vs 69s/$0.57 in evaluation-coverage-assessment, and 0s/$0.00 vs 25s/$0.21 in finish-reason-truncation-drift (the 0s/$0.00 figure suggests without_skill may not have produced a substantive response in that case). Context-window utilization was low and similar for both (roughly 4-7%) with no compactions in any eval.

Overall, with_skill shows a consistent pattern of meeting more expected outputs and passing more assertions, particularly around citing check-ids, distinguishing verified-from-unverifiable claims, and reading failure details before diagnosing — while without_skill runs faster and at lower cost throughout. Given the complete absence of quality-comparison and consistency data, and the medium-confidence nature of several expected-output judgments, this should be read as a directional pattern across these five tasks rather than a definitive quality verdict, and the speed/cost advantage for without_skill is a real tradeoff against its lower assertion pass rates.

evaluation-coverage-assessment.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task. The triggering behavior under test fired successfully (1/1).

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%, high confidence), while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%, medium confidence). Note without_skill's confidence rating here is only "medium," so this finding, while a clear fail on paper, rests on a moderately-confident judgment rather than a highly confident one. with_skill's result is backed by high confidence.

Per-assertion detail (6 assertions total): with_skill passed all 6 (100%), without_skill passed 2 of 6 (33%).
- Two assertions passed for both variants: explaining the production-safety consequence of the current evaluation state, and addressing whether a quality regression can reach production. These two don't differentiate the variants.
- Four assertions passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill: distinguishing "no evaluation configured" from "region doesn't support Bedrock evaluation"; separating what was verified via AWS APIs from what can't be verified (e.g., CI/CD wiring); citing a check id in at least one finding (both an LLM-judged version and a regex-based version of this check). The regex-based check-id assertion is a more objective, non-LLM signal, which adds some confidence to this particular gap, though the LLM-judged assertions on the same theme (confidence "medium" or "low" for without_skill) are weaker measurements.
- No assertion failed for both variants, and none favored without_skill over with_skill.

Metrics: without_skill ran notably faster (24s vs 1m9s for with_skill, roughly 45s difference) and cheaper ($0.20 vs $0.57). Context window utilization was similar and low for both (6.5% vs 7.1%), with no compaction for either.

Quality comparison and output consistency: no data available — the quality comparison pair was skipped (0 pairs evaluated), and output consistency was not measured (null) for both variants. These dimensions provide no evidence either way.

Overall state: On this single task, with_skill passed the expected-output check and all six assertions, while without_skill passed only the two assertions that both variants satisfied and failed the other four, including a regex-verified check-id citation. without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. Since quality-comparison and consistency data are absent, and the sample size is just one task, this should be read as a single-instance finding rather than a broad pattern — but within that one instance, the correctness/assertion gap is consistent and includes at least one non-LLM (regex) signal, while the speed/cost difference represents a real tradeoff in the opposite direction.

finish-reason-truncation-drift.summary:
This was a single chat-task eval. The trigger behavior under test fired successfully (1/1), which applies to the eval generally rather than distinguishing the variants.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%, high confidence), while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%, medium confidence). Note without_skill's miss is based on only a single run and medium-confidence judging, so while it's a clear directional gap, it rests on a thin sample.

Per-assertion detail (5 assertions total) shows a mixed and informative picture rather than a uniform gap:
- One assertion ("concrete cause" explanation) passed for both variants — this assertion isn't differentiating them.
- Two assertions (the finish-reason-logging-requirement statement, and giving both a current and baseline figure) failed for both variants — these indicate a shared gap or an assertion/behavior that neither variant satisfies, rather than a weakness specific to one variant.
- Two assertions (marking the truncation-shift threshold as derived/workload-specific, and marking the finish-reason shift threshold as derived rather than AWS-published) passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill, with without_skill's failures rated low confidence — so these specific gaps are real in direction but weakly measured.

Overall assertion pass rate: with_skill 3/5 (60%), without_skill 1/5 (20%).

Metrics: with_skill took ~25s and cost ~$0.21 per run with 5.0% context utilization; without_skill is recorded at 0s runtime and $0.00 cost with 4.3% context utilization. The 0s/$0 figures for without_skill are unusual and suggest it may not have executed the same way or that data wasn't captured for this run — this should be treated as a measurement gap rather than evidence of a faster/cheaper variant.

Quality comparison: no pairs were actually evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no quality-comparison signal available for this task.

Output consistency: not available (null) for both variants, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall: this is a single-sample comparison with several results resting on low or medium confidence and some missing/anomalous metrics (notably without_skill's zero runtime/cost). Within those limits, with_skill met the expected output and passed more assertions than without_skill on this one task, including two specific assertions about correctly framing thresholds as derived rather than AWS-published. Two other assertions failed for both variants, pointing to a shared gap (around logging-enablement reporting and providing both current/baseline figures) rather than a difference between the variants. No quality or consistency comparison could be made due to skipped/missing data.

quality-regression-triage.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task. The behavior under test ("trigger") fired successfully in the one case tested (1/1, 100%), so the scenario was exercised as intended.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%) while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%). Both confidence ratings for this judgment are "medium," so this is a real but not extremely high-confidence difference — it rests on a single task instance for each variant, so it shouldn't be treated as a large-sample finding.

Assertions: Both variants passed all three individual assertions (3/3, 100% each), with high confidence on every one, and the per-assertion pattern is "always_passes" for all three checks. This means the assertion-level checks (comparing to baseline, addressing A/B comparison, recommending a specific regression gate) did not differentiate the two variants at all — they passed for both, so they don't explain the expected-output gap above. The discrepancy between "both variants pass all assertions" and "without_skill fails the overall expected-output check" suggests the expected-output judgment is evaluating something broader than what the three assertions capture, and that broader criterion is where the two variants diverge.

Metrics: without_skill ran notably faster (6s vs 22s, about 16s less) and cheaper ($0.05 vs $0.19) than with_skill. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (4.4% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either. So without_skill is more efficient on runtime and cost, while with_skill is the one that satisfied the overall expected-output criterion in this single run.

Quality comparison: No quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality beyond the assertion and expected-output checks.

Output consistency: Not measured for either variant (both null), so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability for either variant.

Overall, this is a single-instance comparison with limited data: the only clear differentiator is the expected-output result (with_skill passed, without_skill did not, at medium confidence), while the detailed assertions were uniformly passed by both and quality/consistency data are absent. Separately, without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. These are tradeoffs rather than a clear overall verdict, especially given the small sample size and missing quality/consistency data.

sagemaker-eval-routing-and-failure.summary:
This evaluation is based on a single chat task, so all findings should be read as a limited, single-instance signal rather than a robust trend.

Trigger: the behavior under test fired successfully (1/1).

Expected output: both with_skill and without_skill failed the overall "expected output" check (0/1 each), and this judgment was made with high confidence on both sides. So on this top-line measure, neither variant met the target outcome.

Assertions (finer-grained): here a clearer split emerges. with_skill passed 5 of 6 assertions (83%), while without_skill passed only 1 of 6 (17%). Looking at the individual assertions:
- Four assertions (about confirming SageMaker- vs Bedrock-side evaluation, reading job status/FailureReason instead of guessing, checking whether the artifact was evaluated before promotion, and citing a check-id with a non-mutating remediation command) were passed by with_skill but failed by without_skill, with mostly high (one medium) confidence on with_skill's passes and high confidence on without_skill's failures.
- One regex-based assertion ("at least one finding carries an LLM-SM evaluation check-id") also passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill.
- One regex-based assertion ("no raw 12-digit account ID is exposed") went the other way: without_skill passed and with_skill failed. This is a notable exception showing with_skill has a specific weakness (exposing an account ID) even though it otherwise covered the substantive diagnostic content more thoroughly.

So the assertion-level data shows a consistent pattern favoring with_skill on substantive diagnostic/remediation content, counterbalanced by one data-exposure assertion favoring without_skill.

Metrics: with_skill ran slower (1m13s vs 1m4s, ~9s longer) and cost slightly more ($0.61 vs $0.54), with marginally higher context-window utilization (7.0% vs 5.0%); neither used compaction. These differences are modest in absolute terms.

Quality comparison: no comparable pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct quality-preference signal to weigh here — this dimension is effectively absent data, not a tie or a loss for either variant.

Output consistency: not available for either variant (null), so repeat-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, the picture is mixed and based on a single task: both variants failed the same overall expected-output check, but with_skill passed substantially more individual assertions than without_skill, particularly around diagnostic correctness and remediation guidance, while without_skill uniquely passed the account-ID-exposure assertion that with_skill failed. without_skill was modestly faster and cheaper. There is no quality-comparison or consistency data to add further context, so this should be treated as a narrow, single-instance snapshot rather than a definitive comparison.

bedrock-native-eval-job-failed.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task where the triggering behavior fired successfully (1/1).

Expected output: Neither variant met the expected-output criterion (0/1 for both). Variant_a's failure was judged with "high" confidence, while with_skill's failure was judged with "medium" confidence, so both results indicate a genuine miss against the target, though without_skill's assessment carries the stronger confidence.

Assertions (6 total, independently judged): The two variants' aggregate pass rates differ (with_skill 4/6 = 67% vs without_skill 3/6 = 50%), but breaking this down by individual assertion is more informative than the aggregate:
- Two assertions always fail for both variants ("at least one finding carries an evaluation check-id" and "no raw 12-digit account ID is exposed") — these point to a shared gap (or an overly strict assertion/behavior) rather than a difference between variants.
- Three assertions always pass for both variants (naming concrete configuration causes, correctly treating the job as Bedrock-native rather than SageMaker, and framing remediations as recommended commands without calling mutating APIs) — these are not distinguishing between the variants.
- Exactly one assertion differentiates them: "reads the evaluation job's status and failureMessages before naming a cause," which with_skill passed and without_skill failed (at medium confidence for both). This is the sole evidenced point of difference in behavior.

Metrics: without_skill ran notably faster (~11s vs ~29s) and cheaper (~$0.10 vs ~$0.24) than with_skill, with slightly lower context-window utilization (4.4% vs 6.0%); neither variant triggered any context compaction. These are moderate efficiency differences favoring without_skill, set against with_skill's edge on the one differentiating assertion and on raw assertion pass rate.

Quality comparison: No comparable quality pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so no direct quality-preference signal is available between the variants for this task.

Output consistency: Not measured (null) for both variants, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, this is a single-task, low-volume result. The main evidenced difference is one assertion (evidence-gathering before diagnosis) that with_skill passed and without_skill failed, alongside without_skill's faster and cheaper execution. Both variants missed the overall expected output and both failed the same two assertions, indicating shared weaknesses independent of which variant is considered. With no quality-comparison data and no consistency data available, confidence in any broader conclusion from this single eval should be considered limited.
